newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S., Mexico truckers wary of border opening.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico truckers wary of border opening.

text.p: As the Clinton administration moves closer to allowing Mexican trucks to the cross border and deliver goods in the United States, truckers on both sides of the border are revving up opposition in fear of job losses.

Trucking unions on both sides of the border have opposed the opening, indefinitely postponed by the U.S. government from Dec. 18, 1995, the date set for free truck passage under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

With the U.S. election months gone and president Bill Clinton scheduled to visit Mexico in April or May, analysts expect political factors could compel the United States to let Mexican trucks enter border states in coming weeks.

The delay has been credited to mighty opposition from U.S. unions, jittery that cheap Mexican labor will divert jobs south. Meanwhile, some Mexican companies fear they cannot compete with more modern and efficient U.S. fleets.

"I believe it will be negative to open the border because the economic conditions between the country are very different," vice-president of Mexico's National Chamber of Cargo Transport Alfredo Cardenas told Reuters.

"It will damage Mexicans because no Mexican can compete with the Americans. It should wait until our economy recovers in three to five years more," said Cardenas, also director of the Central de Fletes Monterrey, Mexico's fourth-largest trucking company.

Within the United States and Mexico battle lines are drawn between the unions, which oppose free passage because of job losses, and manufacturers eager for a solution to delays and costly cargo transfers.
"If the Mexicans provide a cheaper and same quality service, what would you do as a shipper?" Texas A&M International University Professor James Giermanski said.

He said an entire business -- known as drayage -- that has flourished on the need to ferry goods from Mexican trucks on one side of the border to U.S. trucks on the other, will also be rendered obsolete if the borders open, putting in risk about 5,000 jobs.
"The truck sits on an unloader, the shipment is torn apart for customs and is reconstituted for transfer to trailers. It's a horrible system," Giermanski said.
He estimated delays because of congestion and paperwork typically last at least eight hours and up to three days. Estimated costs to the industry total millions of dollars per year, he said.

"For many suppliers that buy and sell across the border all the time...and many Mexican companies with large investments in the States, it would be much more convenient, less expensive and quicker if they could drive directly from point of origin to destination," NAFTA consultant David Dean said.
Yet a U.S. decision to open the border to Mexican trucks proabably will not offer a quick fix to border congestion and resentment.

"There's still a strong possibility the Teamsters union will sue and get an injunction to further delay the opening," said Gary Doyle, project legal director for transportation and customs with the National Law Center for Inter-American trade.
The two countries must still agree on standards such as trailer lengths, axel weights, safety and insurance requirements, analysts said.

Because fewer Mexican roads are paved than in the United States, Mexican trucks tend to be heavier. U.S. unions have also claimed Mexican trucks do not conform to U.S. safety standards, a charge vehemently disputed by Mexican companies.
According to the original NAFTA timeline, Mexican and U.S. trucks were supposed to be able to enter only border states until the year 2000, when complete cross-border truck access was to be granted.
Mexico filed a complaint through NAFTA after the delay and analysts said a resolution should be forthcoming.

An estimated 80 percent to 85 percent of cargo between the United States and Mexico travels by highway and through border check points. Most cargo passes through Laredo, Texas, where up to 4,000 trucks cross back and forth the border daily.
